newsitem.title: UK: N. Sea oil could provide more in U.K. tax revenue.
newsitem.headline: N. Sea oil could provide more in U.K. tax revenue.

text.p: Without changes to the current North Sea tax regime, the U.K. will not receive its fair entitlement to profits from offshore oil production, industry analysts said on Monday.

"Oil and gas production is reaching new peaks, but we've seen a rapid decline in the government's share of North Sea profits," Dr Philip Wright of the University of Sheffield told a conference in London.

The U.K. government's share of North Sea oil companies' profits has recently averaged 30 percent, compared to nearly 70 percent in 1987/88, according to a report co-authored by Wright and Dr Ian Rutledge of the University of Sheffield's Energy Studies Programme.

"This has happened despite both a substantial increase in hydrocarbon production since the low of 1989 and a modest, albeit fluctuating recovery in Forties/Brent (crude) prices from the depths which they plumbed in 1986," the report said.
Wright and Rutledge recommend a reintroduction of royalties on North Sea oil and gas production in order to boost state revenue.
Direct pressure from oil companies has brought about numerous changes in the petroleum tax regime since 1983 which have gradually eaten away at the government's share of profits.

These include the abolition of royalties, the doubling of the oil allowance, the introduction of cross-field exploration and development allowances and successive reductions in corporation tax to 33 percent -- lower than in the U.S. and other European countries.
The argument that a lowering of taxes was necessary in order to encourage future production in the U.K. North Sea was rejected by the report.
Worldwide, the U.K. ranks second only to Ireland in terms of fiscal attractiveness to an investing oil company.
And given its good prospectivity and well-developed infrastructure, "the U.K. has the weakest current tax regime in the world," the report said.
This has translated to a recent increase in profitability in the U.K. sector of the North Sea.
"Taking the example of BP, we see a substantial differential enjoyed by BP in North Sea oil and gas compared with the rest of the world," said Wright.
In 1995, British Petroleum reported post-tax profits of 2.31 stg a barrel from its U.K. North Sea operations, compared to 1.30 stg from its operations elsewhere, the report said.
"Many companies are earning 'super-normal' profits from the North sea from what they are currently able to achieve under the tax regimes of other countries," it added.
Some tax incentives should more accurately be termed subsidies, it said.
For instance, according to its 1994 annual report, Lasmo Plc, a medium-sized North Sea producer, was a net recipient of Petroleum Revenue Tax (PRT) prior to 1994.
And analysts Wood Mackenzie estimate that the U.K. tax payer may end up footing the bill for as much as 70 percent of the huge costs of decommissioning North Sea production installations.
"The tax system is in need of refashioning both to simplify things and increase the government's take," said Wright.

The report recommends a reintroduction of royalties on North Sea production as a revenue-raiser, which unlike PRT and corporation tax, can assure the government a specific share of oil and gas profits.
"Above all (royalties) establish that a nation has the right to charge producers for the extraction of its non-renewable mineral wealth." the report said.
--Rosalind Russell, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5387
